- Harry S. Truman: Harry S. Truman (May 8, 1884 – December 26, 1972) was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. A lifetime member of the Democratic Party, he previously served as a U.S. senator from Missouri from 1935 to 1945 and briefly as the 34th vice president in 1945 under President Franklin D. Roosevelt. He succeeded to the presidency on April 12, 1945, upon Roosevelt's death. He implemented the Marshall Plan to rebuild the economy of Western Europe and established the Truman Doctrine and NATO to contain the expansion of communism. He proposed numerous liberal domestic reforms, but few were enacted by the Conservative Coalition that controlled Congress. Truman's presidency was a turning point in foreign affairs, as he largely abandoned the isolationism of the past and committed the U.S. to internationalism. He presided over the end of World War II, the beginning of the Cold War, and the start of the Korean War.
- Nuclear weapon: A nuclear weapon is an explosive device that derives its destructive force from nuclear reactions, either fission (fission bomb) or a combination of fission and fusion reactions (thermonuclear bomb). Both reactions release vast quantities of energy from small amounts of matter. The first test of a fission bomb ("atomic bomb") released an amount of energy equivalent to about 20,000 tons of TNT (84 TJ). The first thermonuclear weapon ("hydrogen bomb") test released an amount of energy equivalent to about 10 million tons of TNT (42 PJ).
- Manhattan Project: The Manhattan Project was a top-secret research and development undertaking by the United States with the support of the United Kingdom and Canada during World War II. Its primary objective was to produce the first nuclear weapons. It was led by the United States Army Corps of Engineers under the direction of Major General Leslie Groves, with theoretical physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer as the scientific director. The project successfully developed and detonated three atomic bombs in 1945: the "Trinity" test bomb, "Little Boy" (used on Hiroshima), and "Fat Man" (used on Nagasaki).
